problem: Persistent behavior-annotated open-vocabulary maps (e.g. VLMM) are assumed to help spatial path planning, and dynamic maps treat when/which entries to re-observe as a fixed schedule or coverage sweep. It is unclear what the map's memory of change is actually useful for.
motivation: Robots have limited perception budgets and cannot re-observe every mapped object, so they must decide what to attend to in order to keep the map fresh. The authors find path-shaping with behavior fields gives a large planning-time gain that mostly vanishes in closed loop, and hypothesize that per-instance change memory pays off in resource allocation instead.
key_idea: Treat budgeted re-perception as an attention (restless-bandit / sqrt-law) decision in which the map's per-instance observed change history, optionally combined with language-derived relevance, sets re-check frequencies.
insight: The memory advantage tracks per-instance heterogeneity Var(sqrt(lambda)) (linear fit R^2=0.99). It appears only when instance rates depart from category norms; under the Whittle index the prior wins at h=0 (-1.2%) and memory wins at h=1 (+4.5%). Much of the large gain over a real CLIP prior is prior mis-calibration (+21% falls to +7-13% after rescaling). Cheap recency often matches memory on the fetch task, and the advantage reverses under poor observation reliability, so the robust claim is only that observation-based scheduling beats a memoryless prior.
method: Staleness objective: each element changes as a Poisson process with rate lambda_i; minimise importance-weighted time-average staleness under a budget of K re-observations per step.
sqrt-law schedule: re-check frequency f_i proportional to sqrt(w_i*lambda_i), realised by an accumulator that re-observes the K highest-credit elements each step.

Memory rate estimate: shrunken estimate lambda_hat=(m_i+kappa*lambda_max*rho_i)/(t_i+kappa) from observed-change counts, evaluated held-out on an independent realisation, versus the memoryless category movability prior from a VLM.

Theory: a Cauchy-Schwarz bound on loss from rate error, and a corollary that the gap over a uniform or homogeneous-prior schedule is proportional to Var(sqrt(lambda)); a closed-form Whittle-index policy is used as the reference scheduler.
Heterogeneity knob h: lambda_i=lambda_max[(1-h)rho_i+h*u_i], interpolating from instance rates equal to the category prior to rates independent of it.

Language-conditioned re-perception: importance w_i is the CLIP relevance of the map feature to a text query, and the schedule uses f_i proportional to sqrt(s_i(q)*lambda_hat_i), combining open-vocabulary grounding with observed dynamics.

setting.backbone: CLIP ViT-B/16 (frozen, laion2b) for movability prior and query relevance; otherwise analytic schedulers (sqrt-law, Whittle index)
setting.training_data: none (training-free; rate estimates accumulated online from simulated observations)
setting.observation: AI2-THOR object instances with rendered views for CLIP and detectability; abstract change-bit observations
setting.action_space: choose K map entries to re-observe per step (abstract attention decision, no low-level actions)
setting.privileged: simulated change process with known ground-truth rates and movability used for oracle comparisons and evaluation; the change dynamics are synthetic

numbers_note: Not a standard navigation benchmark; results are custom simulated staleness and re-perception metrics (e.g. held-out staleness reduction vs category prior, +1.7 to 6.5% over h=0..1; language-conditioned +2.9% over relevance-weighted oldest-first), so no benchmark entries are listed.
results: Held-out change-history memory lowers value-weighted staleness by 1.7-6.5% vs the category prior over h=0..1 (N=951), matches the true-rate sqrt-law oracle, and gives +21-26% against a real CLIP prior (+7-13% after calibration). With language conditioning it beats relevance-weighted oldest-first by +2.9% at h=1 (26 queries) and a category prior by +9.2%. Spatial path-shaping drops from ~35% (planning objective) to ~4% in closed loop.
limitations: The change process and re-observation are simulated and the real-world heterogeneity h is unmeasured; the advantage vanishes or reverses at low heterogeneity, low observation success (<~0.3) and heavy observation noise.
Memory's edge over cheap recency (oldest-first) is small and setting-dependent, reversing at lower heterogeneity in the language task and absent in the generic fetch task.
The sqrt-law is a heuristic (the Whittle index is 4.1% better), and the scheduler ignores travel cost and viewpoint co-visibility.
